title: Delay In Trial No Ground For Bail When Accused Has Criminal Antecedents, Previous Conviction: Supreme Court
case_name: CHANDER PAL v. RAHUL @ VIKRAM & ANR
summary: A mere delay in trial cannot be a ground to enlarge an accused on bail on the strength of his right to a speedy trial while overlooking his antecedents and previous conviction, observed the Supreme Court, while setting aside the bail granted to an accused who had been granted bail in a murder case on the strength of his right to a speedy trial, overlooking his antecedents and previous conviction in an attempt to murder case involving the same deceased person.

note.Facts: A mere delay in trial cannot be a ground to enlarge an accused on bail on the strength of his right to a speedy trial while overlooking his antecedents and previous conviction, observed the Supreme Court, while setting aside the bail granted to an accused who had been granted bail in a murder case on the strength of his right to a speedy trial, overlooking his antecedents and previous conviction in an attempt to murder case involving the same deceased person.
note.Held: Bench: Justice Prashant Kumar Mishra, Justice Shree Chandrashekhar

title: Can Govt Job Be Denied To Selected Candidate Solely Due To Pending Criminal Case? Rajasthan High Court Refers To Larger Bench
case_name: Rajneesh Kumar v. State of Rajasthan & Ors
summary: The Rajasthan High Court has referred to a larger bench the question of whether appointment to public service can be denied to an otherwise meritorious and selected candidate solely on the ground of pendency of a criminal case against them, in the absence of any conviction. Taking note of the divergent views expressed by the Supreme Court as well as different Division Benches of the High.

note.Facts: A meritorious candidate selected for a government post faces denial of appointment solely because a criminal case against him is pending, with no conviction.
note.Issue: Whether a pending criminal case, absent a conviction, can be a ground to refuse appointment to public service.
note.Held: The Rajasthan High Court has referred the question to a larger bench for consideration.
note.Principle: The legality of denying appointment on the basis of pendency of a criminal case, without a conviction, is unsettled and requires authoritative clarification.
note.Exam angle: Service recruitment/appointment under the Constitution/Administrative Law – could be framed as whether the absence of a conviction bars appointment, focusing on the statutory or constitutional criteria for eligibility.

title: JJ Act Amendment Mandating Trial By Children's Courts Has Retrospective Effect: Delhi High Court
summary: The Delhi High Court has held that the 2021 amendment to Section 86(4) of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, which mandates that offences under the Act be tried by a Children's Court, will have retrospective effect and will also apply to trials pending before Judicial Magistrates of First Class. A Division Bench comprising Justice Navin Chawla and Justice.

note.Facts: The Delhi High Court examined the 2021 amendment to Section 86(4) of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, which requires that offences under the Act be tried by a Children’s Court, and considered its applicability to cases already pending before Judicial Magistrates of First Class.
note.Issue: Whether the 2021 amendment to Section 86(4) of the JJ Act has retrospective effect and can be applied to trials already underway before Judicial Magistrates of First Class.
note.Held: The Court held that the amendment is retrospective and will apply to pending trials before Judicial Magistrates of First Class.
note.Principle: An amendment to a procedural provision of the Juvenile Justice Act, specifically mandating trial by Children’s Courts, operates retrospectively and governs cases already in progress.
note.Provisions: Section 86(4) of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 (as amended in 2021); not stated any other statutes or cases.
note.Exam angle: Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 – amendment to Section 86(4); could be asked on the retrospective operation of statutory amendments and the requirement that offences under the Act be tried by Children’s Courts.

title: Person Named In Suicide Note Can't Be Charged With Abetment Solely On Allegations Of Harassment: Rajasthan High Court
case_name: Gopal Kansara & Ors. v. State of Rajasthan & Ors
ratio: Mere allegations of harassment against a person named in a suicide note cannot sustain a charge of abetment of suicide unless the allegations disclose the…
summary: The Rajasthan High Court has held that mere allegations of harassment against a person named in a suicide note cannot sustain a charge of abetment of suicide unless the allegations disclose the essential ingredients of the offence, including intentional instigation. The bench of Justice Farjand Ali observed that allegations of harassment arising out of a property dispute.

note.Facts: The deceased’s suicide note named a person and alleged harassment arising from a property dispute and threats.
note.Issue: Whether mere allegations of harassment in a suicide note suffice to constitute abetment of suicide.
note.Held: The court held that such allegations do not sustain a charge of abetment of suicide unless they disclose the essential ingredients of the offence, including intentional instigation.
note.Principle: A charge of abetment of suicide requires proof of intentional instigation; mere allegations of harassment without such proof are insufficient.

title: TN Govt Moves Madras High Court Against Former Minister K Ponmudi's Acquittal In Alleged Red Sand Mining Case
summary: Justice V Lakshminarayanan has issued notice to Ponmudi and other accused in an application filed by the State seeking to condone a delay of 166 days in filing the appeal.

note.Facts: The Tamil Nadu State filed an application before the Madras High Court seeking to condone a 166-day delay in filing an appeal against the Sessions Court’s order acquitting former DMK minister K Ponmudi and others in an alleged red-sand-mining case. Justice V Lakshminarayanan issued notice to Ponmudi and the other accused.
note.Issue: Whether the High Court should entertain the State’s request to condone the 166-day delay in filing the appeal against the acquittal.
note.Held: The Court issued notice to the respondents, indicating that the application for condoning the delay will be heard.
note.Principle: A High Court may entertain an application for condonation of delay in filing an appeal and must issue notice to the opposite party before deciding the matter.

title: FIR Lodged Against TVK MLA For Sending Obscene Messages To District Collector: Tamil Nadu Police Informs Madras High Court
summary: The court was hearing a plea by a woman advocate seeking directions to the DGP and the Superintendent of Police to register an FIR against and conduct a fair, impartial, and expeditious investigation in the matter.

note.Facts: An FIR was registered against TVK MLA Arul Vignesh for allegedly sending obscene WhatsApp messages to the Kallakurichi District Collector and allegedly trespassing at her official residence.
note.Issue: Whether the police and the State must register an FIR, conduct an impartial investigation, and constitute a POSH-Act Internal Complaints Committee when a woman officer’s dignity is allegedly affronted by an elected representative.
note.Held: The Madras High Court directed the police to file a final report by 22 December, to constitute an Internal Complaints Committee under the POSH Act, and to ensure proactive removal of the obscene posts; it emphasized that senior police officials must oversee the investigation.
note.Principle: When an allegation of sexual harassment or obscene communication involves a woman officer, the State must ensure a prompt FIR, an impartial investigation, and compliance with the POSH Act’s requirement of an Internal Complaints Committee, irrespective of the accused’s status.
note.Provisions: POSH Act (reference to Internal Complaints Committee); not stated – no specific sections or case law cited in the source.
note.Exam angle: Questions may be framed on the applicability of the POSH Act to public officials and the duty of police under criminal procedure to register FIRs and conduct unbiased investigations when women’s dignity is at stake.

title: Thiruparankundram Deepam Row: Madras High Court Agrees To Urgently Hear Pleas Against Prohibitory Orders In Madurai
summary: The Madras High Court has agreed to urgently hear a batch of pleas challenging the prohibitory orders imposed in Madurai under Section 163 BNSS, in connection with the lighting of Karthigai Deepam in Thiruparankundram.

note.Facts: The Madurai District Collector issued prohibitory orders under Section 163 BNSS to bar public assembly for the lighting of Karthigai Deepam at Thiruparankundram; devotees and officials filed pleas seeking permission to assemble and conduct the ritual.
note.Issue: Whether the prohibitory orders under Section 163 BNSS can be set aside to allow the lighting of the lamp and limited public presence.
note.Held: The Madras High Court agreed to hear the batch of pleas urgently and summoned the Collector and Police Commissioner, indicating a willingness to examine the validity of the prohibitory orders.
note.Principle: A court may entertain urgent petitions challenging prohibitory orders under Section 163 BNSS when they affect religious rites, balancing public order with constitutional freedom of religion.
note.Provisions: Section 163 BNSS; Supreme Court judgment (Justice Aravind Kumar & Justice Vipul M Pancholi) staying the Madras High Court’s earlier order; Madras High Court’s earlier judgment permitting lighting (now stayed).

title: Thiruparankundram Karthigai Deepam | Implement SC Order, Review Pendency No Ground For Non-Compliance : Madras High Court To Authorities
ratio: The prohibitory order issued by Madurai Collector in the area cannot come in the way of exercise of fundamental rights of the devotees
summary: The Madras High Court on Tuesday (November 24) directed Madurai Collector and other authorities to comply with Supreme Court's order permitting lighting of the lamp for Karthigai Deepam celebrations at Thiruparankundram today.

note.Facts: The Madurai District Collector issued a prohibitory order under Section 163 BNSS to prevent unauthorised persons from climbing the hill at Thiruparankundram during Karthi gai Deepam. Petitioners claimed the order obstructed the Supreme Court’s November 20 order permitting the lighting of the lamp and infringed devotees’ right to worship.
note.Issue: Whether the Collector’s prohibitory order can be enforced despite the Supreme Court’s direction allowing the lamp-lighting ceremony and whether pending review of the Supreme Court order is a ground for non-compliance.
note.Held: The Madras High Court directed the Collector and all other authorities to comply with the Supreme Court order; the prohibitory order cannot override the Supreme Court’s direction, and pending review is not a ground for non-compliance. Unlawfully detained persons must be released.
note.Principle: A prohibitory order issued by a civil authority must yield to a Supreme Court order; under Article 144, all authorities in India are bound to act in aid of the Supreme Court, and such orders cannot curtail fundamental rights under Article 25.
note.Exam angle: Questions may test the interplay between Article 144 (obligation of authorities to obey Supreme Court orders) and Article 25 (freedom of religion), or ask to identify the statutory provision (Section 163 BNSS) that cannot be invoked to defeat a Supreme Court direction.

title: Madras High Court Gags Media From Publishing Details of Sexual Harassment Case Against Kallakurichi MLA
summary: The Madras High Court, on Tuesday (November 24), has issued a gag order restraining the media from publishing information relating to the sexual harassment case involving Kallakurichi MLA Arul.

note.Facts: The Madras High Court restrained media from publishing any details of a sexual-harassment case involving Kallakurichi MLA Arul Vignesh, after widespread publicity and an FIR was filed for obscene messages sent to a woman officer.
note.Issue: Whether the press and social-media platforms may be enjoined from disclosing the contents of the complaint and inquiry under the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013.
note.Held: The court issued an interim injunction prohibiting publication of any matter covered by Section 16 of the PoSH Act and directed removal of related posts, with police monitoring for violations.
note.Principle: Publication of the contents of a sexual-harassment complaint or inquiry proceedings is prohibited under Section 16 of the PoSH Act, and the court may enforce this by restraining the media and ordering removal of offending material.
note.Provisions: Section 16 of the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013; no other statutes or cases cited.
note.Exam angle: PoSH Act – focus on Section 16’s prohibition on publishing complaint details; could be asked on the scope of media injunctions and the court’s power to enforce confidentiality in sexual-harassment proceedings.

Thiruparankundram Deepam Row: Madras High Court Asks State To Reconsider Prohibitory Orders In Madurai, Cites Devotees' Article 25 Rights
summary: The Madras High Court (Madurai Bench) on Tuesday (November 24) asked the Tamil Nadu government to reconsider the prohibitory orders imposed in Madurai in connection with the Karthigai Deepam celebrations at Thiruparankundram, observing that the restrictions could impede devotees' right to practise and profess religion under Article 25 of the Constitution of India.

note.Facts: The Madurai Collector issued prohibitory orders under Section 163 BNSS restricting assemblies for the Karthigai Deepam lighting at Thiruparankundram, despite a Supreme Court order permitting a one-time lighting on 24 Nov.
note.Issue: Whether the State’s prohibitory orders can stand when they impede devotees’ right to practise religion under Article 25 of the Constitution.
note.Held: The Madras High Court directed the State to reconsider the prohibitory orders, emphasizing they must not obstruct the exercise of Article 25 rights and must implement the Supreme Court’s directive.
note.Principle: A State may not enforce prohibitory orders that curtail the fundamental right to freedom of religion (Art 25) where a higher court has authorised the religious activity; the higher court’s order must be implemented.
note.Provisions: Article 25 Constitution of India; Section 163 BNSS (Tamil Nadu) – as cited in the pleadings; Supreme Court order permitting one-time lighting of the lamp.
note.Exam angle: Questions may arise under the Constitution (Article 25) on the limits of state-imposed restrictions on religious practice, testing the interplay between statutory prohibitions (Section 163 BNSS) and Supreme Court directives.

title: Indian Student In Russia Joins Russian Army; Supreme Court Seeks Centre's Response On Father's Plea For His Return
summary: A bench of CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana passed the order in the petitioner-father's plea, asking Solicitor General Tushar Mehta to intervene in the matter obtain instructions.
